en: So when we're talking about inference,
there is an approach called quantization
that can make running
models, large models, a bit more
approachable and efficient. Because these
weights in these models, these weights that
connect the different parameters,
they
are quite long numbers, to put it bluntly.
They are so-called 16-bit floating point
numbers very often, which means
long numbers with decimal places with a lot
of precision.
Now, all these numbers take up memory. It
may just look like an innocent number, but
it takes up space and memory, and there are
lots of those numbers in complex models. We
have trillions of parameters that need to be
connected after all.
Now, if we would reduce the precision of
these weights, if we would cut them off, so
to say,
we could therefore save space in memory
because the longer a number is, the more
precisely a number is stored, the more space
it takes up in memory. And the idea behind
quantization is all about truncating those
numbers, cutting them off,
losing some precision, and therefore saving
some memory. Now, with less precision, you
also lose some quality. The responses can
get worse, but research has shown that it's
quite a small
loss in quality for quite a large gain in
memory savings.
So especially when we're talking about
serving models locally, running models
locally on your machine, it's quite common
to use so-called quantized versions of these
models, which are a bit worse but require
far less memory. And therefore quantization
is something that makes serving models much
more approachable.
